title: Increment, decrement, bitwise, ternary, and special operators
sourceLabel: Operators: Increment and Decrement, Bitwise, Ternary and Special Operators.
objectives: Trace ++ and -- in prefix and postfix form on a single variable.
Explain bitwise & | ^ ~ << >> as operations on bits, with a tiny example.
Evaluate the ternary operator c ? a : b.
Name common special operators used in first year: sizeof, comma, and (preview) & and *.
State when a construct is standard C versus implementation-defined.
completionCriteria: Trace one prefix and one postfix example correctly.
Evaluate a ternary with a known condition.
Knowledge checks passed. Do not claim mastery of bitwise exam tricks beyond the supplied examples.

notes.introduction: The lesson-plan title groups four leftover operator families. We treat each family separately so they do not blur. Bitwise work is still just 0 and 1 from topic 1.
notes.beginner: ++ adds one to a variable. -- subtracts one. Written before the name (++n) it changes n first, then uses the new value. Written after (n++) it uses the old value, then changes n. Bitwise operators look at each bit: & both 1, | at least one 1, ^ different bits, ~ flip, << shift left, >> shift right. The ternary operator is a short if: condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false. Special operators in this college list usually include sizeof (size in bytes), the comma operator, and sometimes & (address) and * (indirection) — those last two are previewed only.
notes.formal: Prefix ++/-- increment or decrement the operand and yield the updated value. Postfix ++/-- yield the previous value and update the operand as a side effect. Bitwise operators apply independently to each bit of the integer representation. The conditional operator ?: is the only ternary operator in C. sizeof yields the size in bytes of a type or expression as a size_t. Shifting a negative value or shifting by a width greater than the type is undefined or implementation-defined; first-year examples should use small non-negative ints and modest shift counts.

terms.meaning: Each bit is 1 only if both sides have 1. Different from &&.
Choose one of two values using a condition.
Standard operator. Result is the size in bytes. Do not memorise a magic number for int; it can differ between machines.
Evaluate left, then right; the value is the right. Rare in clear beginner code.

revision: ++n versus n++ — when is n used?
cond ? a : b chooses a if cond is non-zero.
sizeof is standard C. Exact byte sizes are not a promise of this course.
notes.examAnswer: ++ and -- increment or decrement; prefix updates before the value is used, postfix after. Bitwise operators manipulate bits. The ternary operator selects between two expressions. Special operators include sizeof and comma. Use only well-defined shifts on non-negative values in this course.

body.objectives: You should trace ++/-- without a computer, evaluate one ternary, and compute 5 & 3 and 5 | 3 on paper.
body.prerequisiteCheck: You must be solid on = versus == and on && versus a single &. Reopen topic 6 if those still mix.
body.introduction: These operators look small and cause large exam mistakes. We go slowly. We will not stack many ++ in one line — that is hard to read and can be undefined if the same variable is modified twice without a sequence point. First-year style: one change per statement.
body.analogy: A turnstile counter is ++: one more person. Prefix is 'add, then tell me the new number'. Postfix is 'tell me the number you had, then add'. Bitwise is two rows of light switches; & turns a light on only if both rows have that switch on. Ternary is a fork in a path with exactly two destinations.
body.explanation:
Increment and decrement. int n = 5; ++n; now n is 6. n--; now n is 5. The useful distinction is inside a larger expression. int n = 5; int a = ++n; n becomes 6, a is 6. int n = 5; int b = n++; b is 5, then n becomes 6. After both stories n is 6, but a and b differ. Do not write n++ * ++n. The standard does not define that.

Bitwise, using 4-bit teaching pictures (the extra high bits are 0). 5 is 0101. 3 is 0011. 5 & 3 is 0001 = 1. 5 | 3 is 0111 = 7. 5 ^ 3 is 0110 = 6 (bits that differ). ~ on a signed int is more than first-year need; we only say it flips every bit and the decimal result depends on the width and representation. << 1 on a non-negative value multiplies by two when no 1 falls off the left: 3 << 1 is 6. >> 1 on a non-negative value divides by two: 6 >> 1 is 3. Shifts of negative values or huge counts are not used in this lesson.

Ternary. int marks = 42; int pass = (marks >= 40) ? 1 : 0; pass is 1. It is an expression, so it produces a value. It is not a replacement for every if; long branches should stay as if in Unit 2.

Special operators. sizeof(int) is an integer number of bytes on that machine — do not hard-code 4 in an exam answer unless the question gives the size. The comma operator in x = (a=1, a+2); sets a to 1 then yields 3. Prefer two statements. &variable is the address (you already used it in scanf). *pointer is indirection — named only so the symbol is not a surprise; Unit 4 will teach it properly.

All of ++ -- ?: sizeof comma & * and the bitwise operators discussed here are standard C. We are not using a compiler-specific rotate intrinsic or a non-standard bitwise method.
body.syntax:
++n n++ --n n--
bitwise: a&b a|b a^b ~a a<<k a>>k
ternary: cond ? expr_true : expr_false
sizeof(type)  sizeof expr
Keep ++/-- on their own line when you are learning.

body.execution: Trace int n=2; int m = ++n * 3; ++n makes n=3 first, then 3*3=9, m is 9. Trace int n=2; int m = n++ * 3; uses 2*3=6 for m, then n becomes 3.

trace.prompt: int n=5; int a=++n; What are a and n? Write two integers.

predict.prompt: What is 5 & 3 as a decimal integer?

mistakes: Believing sizeof(int) is always 4 on every computer.
Shifting by 40 on a 32-bit int. That is not a first-year toy example; it is undefined or meaningless.

guided.prompt: 5 | 3 equals which decimal? Type the integer.

check.prompt: int n=1; printf("%d", n++); What is printed?
Decimal value of 6 >> 1 (non-negative shift as in the lesson).

body.summary: ++/-- change by one; prefix versus postfix is about when the value is used. Bitwise works per bit and is not && ||. Ternary chooses a value. sizeof and comma are special; & and * are previewed. Stay inside well-defined, small examples.
